prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: B013 is a clear invention with a clear experimental fingerprint. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trade-off between long interrogation of many atoms and light-shift and Doppler perturbations, and Ye's group turned it into the record-accuracy and record-stability instrument at about 1e-18, using stabilised lasers, frequency combs and many-body control. The consequences are concrete and testable: comparisons between independent laboratories, relativistic geodesy, bounds on drifts of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, and the coming redefinition of the second. Four colleagues ranked it in their top five and two put it first, and the two-name credit is compact and unusually well defined. The prize would also answer the question of what limits what we can measure, which in my view is the right kind of criterion for an experimental prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest counterargument is breadth and balance. The 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control) sit close to this work, and some will see a clock prize as a third helping of precision metrology. Ye's contributions are broad, which can make a Katori/Ye split look uneven, and the case rests partly on the redefinition of the second, which has not happened. Against B041, the topological-insulator candidate has stronger opening support (four first places) and a larger conceptual reach across condensed matter. If my colleagues judge that conceptual reorganisation outweighs instrumental invention, B041 is the more defensible first choice, and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B041 first because it is a clear discovery with an experimental fingerprint, and would give the three slots to Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, leaving Mele out.
responses.response: I share the criterion, and I think B013 meets it as well: a magic-wavelength lattice gives a measured number, a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 that independent laboratories reproduce and compare. I accept that the topological-insulator case is conceptually broader. My reservation is attribution. A three-name split that omits Mele, whose work with Kane is the origin of the Z2 idea, is a serious problem, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal sits outside the credited names. B013 has no comparable gap. I would still rank B041 as the strongest alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first as an original, clean idea that took optical frequency standards well beyond caesium, with the comb and ion-clock prizes as context for timing.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the attribution. Her point on timing is the one I take most seriously. The comb and ion-clock prizes do not cover the lattice clock, since the magic-wavelength idea and the many-atom stability gain are new, but they mean we should write the citation narrowly around the lattice scheme and its accuracy, not around clocks in general. I would also not lean on the redefinition of the second as part of the justification, because it has not happened. The physics already stands on the comparisons.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the theta13 measurement (B018) first as a decisive precision experiment with a clean signal, confirmed by Daya Bay, RENO, Double Chooz and T2K.
responses.response: I agree it is a decisive measurement and that confirmation is complete. But it carries the hardest attribution problem on the shortlist: reactor and accelerator results, three collaborations, and three leaders, with the credit spread across large teams. It also received no first place from anyone but him, and the 2015 oscillation prize covers the neighbouring ground. B013 offers a comparable measurement-driven case with a much cleaner credit. If Pearce can show that Luk, Wang and Nishikawa is defensible, I would listen, but I do not see it overtaking the two leading candidates.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B029 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) first, with the quantum anomalous Hall realisation as a second experimental pillar alongside HgTe, and puts B013 only fifth.
responses.response: I think B029 gives a good trio on paper, but it splits the topological vote with B041 and mixes two experimental claims. The quantum anomalous Hall effect is a real result but younger and still limited by temperature, so it is the less mature part. If the committee goes topological, I would prefer one coherent configuration with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp over one that adds Xue. As for ranking B013 fifth, I would ask what the objection is. Is it the earlier metrology prizes, or the credit?

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees a lattice-clock prize as too close to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether the Katori/Ye pair omits Lemonde, Takamoto or others who made early strontium lattice measurements.
How much weight the committee gives to a redefinition of the second that has not yet happened.
Whether topological insulators deserve priority from the committee's broader first-place support, and how to split their credit among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory, and Ye's career is closely tied to Hall's group; I also work in laser stabilisation and precision laser spectroscopy, which are inputs to lattice clocks, so a personal and field connection to B013 may deserve discussion for possible recusal. No specific connection to any other shortlisted candidate is apparent from the provided profile.
